title: "Started successfully" only proves root's part worked
explanation: nginx's master process runs as root, and root ignores standard file read/write permission checks entirely. So `sudo service nginx start` reporting success tells you the master could bind port 80 and parse its config — it tells you nothing about whether the unprivileged workers that actually serve files can read them.

title: The status code is your first real clue
explanation: A 403 is meaningfully different from a timeout or connection-refused: it means a live process received the request and deliberately refused it. For a plain static-file server, a 403 (as opposed to a 404 or 500) points squarely at the filesystem — the process can see the file but isn't allowed to read it.

title: Root's workers deliberately aren't root
explanation: Production daemons that bind a privileged port as root (nginx, most web/mail servers) typically drop privileges for the processes that actually touch untrusted input and user-facing files — so a compromised worker can't do root-level damage. That design choice means the permission boundary you actually have to satisfy is the worker's identity (`www-data`), not root's.

title: Confirm the gap empirically before changing anything
explanation: `ls -la /var/www/html` shows the directory at `700` and the file at `600`, both `root:root` — `www-data` has zero bits set on either, so it can't even traverse into the directory, let alone open the file. Verifying this directly matters because a 403 could in principle have other causes; seeing the exact missing bits confirms this one and tells you precisely what to grant.

title: Grant the minimum the worker actually needs
explanation: `chmod 755` on the directory (adds traverse+read for others) and `chmod 644` on the file (adds read for others) restores exactly what an unprivileged reader needs — not a blanket `777` that would loosen far more than the problem requires.

title: Verify as the actor that was failing, not as root
explanation: Checking with `sudo cat` or as root would lie to you, since root bypasses the very check you're trying to validate. The correct verification is `curl localhost` — the same unprivileged path a real visitor's request takes — now returning a 200.
